name: PT Armada Berjaya Trans Tbk

frontmatter.title: Armada Berjaya Trans: a leased fleet whose cash flow does not cover its claim
frontmatter.summary: The 2026 step-change is filed, but it was bought with IDR143.6bn of finance leases against IDR135.0bn of equity, and the reinvestment it carries leaves the discounted cash flow worth less than the debt it deducts. The published target is carried by the earnings multiples, not by the cash flow. We remain at SELL, target Rp84, -32.0% — a higher target than the previous version, because the construction is fixed, not because the outlook has improved.
thesis: The step-change is filed, not forecast: nine-month revenue of IDR97.3bn against IDR53.4bn, land transport IDR91.8bn and net profit IDR10.7bn [S2].
It was bought with leases: net fixed assets of IDR369.9bn and finance lease liabilities of IDR143.6bn at September 2026 against equity of IDR135.0bn [S2].

The asset base is close to three times FY2026E revenue against roughly one times in FY2024, so depreciation is 30.0% of revenue and gross capex 110.0% in FY2026E against 28.0% at the end, leaving free cash flow of IDR-94.6bn in FY2026E and IDR10.8bn in FY2027E [S2][S4].

On a 12.0% WACC the DCF enterprise value is IDR110.0bn, less than the net debt it deducts at the pack's 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date; the cash-flow leg floors at nil and the weighted value of Rp39 comes from the earnings legs at Rp27 and Rp212 [S0].
The market pays 10.9x our FY2026E earnings and 0.7x book for a 7.1% return on equity, on contracts whose term and volume are not disclosed [S0][S2].
The bear case is a lost contract at 35% probability and the bull a filled fleet at 20%; only the bull moves the target, because the bear is bounded by the DCF floor [S0].

blocks.text: This is a revision answering the quality-control audit, and it keeps the thesis but corrects its construction. We rate PT Armada Berjaya Trans Tbk (JAYA) **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp84**, or -32.0% from the Rp124 at which the shares last traded, with no dividend assumed in the next twelve months (Rp0) [S0]. Four corrections drove the change, and each was required by the evidence rather than by a change of mood.

The balance sheet is now one roll and not two. The model rolls debt from the pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet instead of from end-2025: total debt reaches IDR223.8bn at the end of FY2026E — the June actual plus the second-half lease increment — and FY2027E charges IDR21.1bn of interest on it at the 9.4% cost of debt used in the WACC [S0][S2]. The DCF discounts from the same June date with its first year prorated from it, so its flows already carry the second-half capex, and it deducts the net debt at that date with no bridge; the earlier version deducted the September liabilities on top of those flows, which counted the same investment twice.

The reinvestment is unchanged in direction and now stated as a convention. Capex is gross fleet additions, lease-funded included, because the lease liability sits in net debt: 110.0% of revenue in FY2026E, falling to 28.0% once the fleet is in place [S2]. That is the cautious of the two available conventions — the alternative charges only cash capex and treats the lease as a perpetual rollover — and the bull case is where that difference is recovered. The asset base is IDR369.9bn of net fixed assets against FY2026E revenue of IDR133.3bn, close to three times revenue where the FY2024 fleet carried roughly one times, so the depreciation charge is 30.0% of revenue and the cash the business keeps after keeping the fleet whole is a small fraction of the EBITDA line [S2][S4].

The method follows the industry, and the legs now run on live inputs rather than on a stale trailing year. The DCF carries 60% because the economics are a fleet, a maintenance cycle and a lease obligation; its enterprise value of IDR110.0bn is below the net debt it deducts, so the leg floors at nil. The EV/EBITDA leg carries 25% at 8.1x of own history and returns Rp27; the P/E keeps 15% at 15.7x and returns Rp212, above the price, because a P/E ignores the debt [S0]. The weighted value is Rp39 a share, rolled forward one year at a cost of equity of 21.2% to Rp47, scenario-weighted to Rp94, less a 10% discount for a 25.7% free float and IDR1,569.9m of daily turnover, giving Rp84 [S0].

The variant view is about the price, not the story. At Rp124 the market pays 10.9x our FY2026E earnings and 0.7x book, for a business whose return on equity is 7.1% and whose free cash flow is IDR-94.6bn in the first forecast year [S0][S2]. The market is not paying for the filed step-change; it has already seen it. It is paying for a utilisation assumption — that IDR369.9bn of trucks earn the revenue per unit that the 2024 fleet earned — which the company has not disclosed a contract to support [S2][S4].

Three things move the value, and only one of them is a growth story. Customer concentration is the first: the largest customer supplied 34.3% of nine-month revenue and the two largest together close to half, on terms that are not disclosed [S2]. Maintenance is the second: we fade the gross margin from 47.7% in FY2027E to 45.3% by FY2030E as the 2025-26 trucks reach their first heavy cycle [S4]. The lease book is the third: IDR143.6bn of finance lease liabilities carried IDR11.3bn of interest in nine months against pre-tax profit of IDR11.3bn, and the interest charge is a fixed claim ahead of the shareholder [S2].

The scenarios are wide, and only one of them moves the target. If one of the two large contracts is lost at renewal the fleet stays but the gross profit does not, and we put that at 35%; if the fleet is filled on multi-year contracts the same assets earn far more, which we put at 20%; the base case is the filed run-rate extended, at 45% [S0]. The base and the bear both value the equity at Rp47, because the DCF is already floored at nil and the earnings legs are struck on trailing figures the shocks cannot reach: that is a floor, not a forecast. The bull lifts the DCF above the obligations and values the equity at Rp281, and it is what carries the probability-weighted target to Rp94. We state the asymmetry rather than hide it: the downside is bounded by the floor, the upside by the contracts.

JAYA is a Jakarta-based land transport and logistics operator. It was incorporated as PT Armada Beton, a cement-mixer transporter, and shifted into general land transport in 2015 before taking its present name in 2018 and listing in 2019 [S5]. The service range is the standard middle of the Indonesian road-freight market: container and loose-cargo haulage, long-box and CDD box trucks, blind vans, customs clearance, warehousing and domestic door-to-door delivery [S5][S0]. The customer proposition is business-to-business haulage for large corporates rather than parcel or last-mile work [S3].

Capacity is the business. At the end of 2024 the company operated 226 units — trailers, drop-side trucks, CDD box trucks and blind vans — supported by 172 driver partners, with all units emission-tested and maintained at partner workshops [S3]. The driver relationship matters to the economics: the company reports 44.0 employees, so the driving workforce is engaged as partners rather than payroll, which converts a fixed labour cost into a variable one and shifts wage pressure into the gross margin rather than the opex line [S0][S3]. Fleet additions are the growth mechanism, and they are lumpy: gross fixed-asset additions were IDR67.5bn in FY2024, of which a large part was finance-lease assets, against disposals of old units in the same year [S4].

Revenue is overwhelmingly land transport, with a small property tail. Of IDR100.7bn of FY2024 revenue, land transport contributed IDR89.5bn, villa rental IDR6.1bn and subsidised housing sales IDR5.1bn [S4]. The shape is similar in the nine months to September 2026, when land transport produced IDR91.8bn, rental services about a nineteenth of that, and property sales a rounding item [S2]. The property tail is small but real: the group owns investment property at a cost of IDR52.7bn, largely commercial buildings and land in Bali plus work in progress, and rents it out for a yield that is disclosed separately in the revenue note [S4].

The customer book has been both concentrated and, until recently, related. In FY2024 four customers each supplied more than a tenth of revenue and together accounted for 49.8% of the total; the largest of them was PT Prima Globalindo Logistik Tbk, the controlling shareholder, at 16.7% of revenue [S3][S4]. The transport agreement with PGL ran to the end of 2025, and the financial statements say plainly that related-party terms may differ from those available to unrelated parties [S4]. The 2026 step-change has changed the names: PT Nusantara Ekspres Kilat supplied 34.3% of nine-month revenue (IDR33.5bn) and PT Global Optimus Prime Logistik supplied roughly an eighth, so the two largest customers accounted for close to half of revenue against two thirds a year earlier [S2]. Concentration is lower and the related party is no longer the largest customer. On affiliation we can only report what the filings support, and we have labelled the rest as unverified rather than asserting it either way: Nusantara Ekspres Kilat appears in the trade-receivable note as a third-party balance in both the FY2024 accounts and the half-year 2025 accounts, which is the filings' own classification of it as unrelated [S4][S6]; Global Optimus Prime Logistik does not appear in those notes at all, because the relationship is new, and nothing in the registry establishes who owns it — the name shares the words Global, Prime and Logistik with the controlling shareholder PT Prima Globalindo Logistik, which is suggestive and no more than that [S4]. If Global Optimus is an affiliate, related-party revenue is already close to a fifth of the total, not a rounding item; we treat that as an open question and it is one of the reasons the bear case is not a tail we dismiss. The new book is young and its contract terms are not disclosed.

Strategy is straightforward and has not changed with the cycle: target large corporate shippers in food and beverage, industrial and textile sectors, keep the fleet adequate to the contracts, add medium and small units as customer drop sizes change, and compete on punctuality, cargo security and price rather than on technology [S3]. The company added CDD units in 2024 specifically to serve that corporate base [S3]. The 2025 plan was to grow revenue to IDR110.8bn and net profit above the prior year; revenue came in at IDR73.9bn, below plan, and net profit fell, which tells you how much of the strategy depends on contracts landing [S3].

The property arm sits under two subsidiaries, PT Aman Bae Sentosa and PT Aman Bae Perkasa, which develop subsidised housing at Cibarusah in Bekasi and commercial property in Bali [S3]. Management links the segment to the government's mass-housing programme and to the housing backlog, and funds it with capital and management support from the parent [S3]. It is not the reason to own the shares, but it is not worthless either: IDR52.7bn of investment property at cost and a rental stream of roughly IDR6.1bn a year are carried inside a market capitalisation of IDR97,897.9m, and our DCF credits their cash flow rather than their book value.

Ownership is concentrated and family-controlled. At the end of 2024 PT Prima Globalindo Logistik Tbk held the largest block, the President Director held a substantial personal stake and the President Commissioner held a further block, with the public holding the residual; the annual report identifies the President Director as the ultimate beneficial owner because he also controls PGL [S3]. On the exchange's registry the insider share is 74.3% and the free float 25.7% [S0]. JAYA is therefore a controlled micro-cap whose controlling shareholder was also a customer and is a listed company in its own right — a structure we return to in the governance section.

Position in the value chain is that of a challenger with a good reputation and no scale advantage. The company describes itself as one of the better-regarded operators with a base of loyal corporate customers, which is the honest description of a niche carrier [S3]. Against national fleets and the large listed logistics groups its 226 units are small, and the exchange's own ranking places it in the bottom quarter of its industry by market capitalisation [S5]. The moat, such as it is, is the relationship and the service record with a handful of shippers, plus a fleet that is already compliant and already financed; it is not route density, brand or switching cost.

The company does not disclose the size of its addressable market, and the annual report's industry section is built on national accounts rather than on a freight-market estimate, so we do not pretend to a market-share number [S3]. What the filing does give is the direction of travel: the transportation and warehousing sector grew by nearly nine per cent in the official data cited for 2024, down from a much stronger rate in 2023, while manufacturing grew more slowly than the economy as a whole and inflation stayed low [S3]. Road freight is a derivative of manufacturing output, construction and trade volumes, so a year in which manufacturing undershoots GDP is a year in which haulage rates are weak and competition for volume is sharp.

Demand is broad but not deep. JAYA's customer base spans food and beverage, industrial and textile shippers, a fair cross-section of the consumer and export-exposed manufacturing economy, and the fleet mix it is buying — more CDD and medium units, fewer very large trailers — reflects smaller drop sizes and more frequent deliveries [S3]. That shift favours carriers able to add standard box capacity quickly, which is exactly what a lease-financed fleet allows.

Competition is fragmented and getting more so. The annual report is explicit that competition intensified in 2024 as more operators entered the market and that tariff competition became tighter as a result [S3]. There is no disclosed market share, no published rate card and no long-term contract disclosure in the financial statements, so the competitive position has to be inferred from margin and customer behaviour rather than measured. On that evidence JAYA is a price-taker in a market where the minimum efficient scale is one truck and a leasing contract: any shipper with a credit line can replicate the capacity, and the truck arrives with much the same financing terms available to JAYA itself.

The five forces are unfavourable on three of them. Buyer power is high: two customers supplied close to half of nine-month revenue and four supplied half of FY2024 revenue, and a shipper of that size can tender its haulage annually [S2][S3]. Supplier power is moderate and rising with the lease book: the fleet is bought on finance leases from a small group of lessors, and the FY2024 accounts name the lessors and disclose effective rates across a wide band, which is the profile of a borrower without much bargaining power [S4]. Rivalry is high because the service is undifferentiated and rates are the main variable. The threat of new entrants is high for the same reason. Only the threat of substitutes is low: rail and sea can take long-haul volume, but distribution to warehouses and factories in Java is a road product.

Regulation cuts both ways and is a named risk in the company's own register. The annual report lists government policy as a risk, specifically because rules change — it cites Jakarta traffic regulation as an example — and because compliance costs fall on the operator [S3]. The fleet must pass emission tests, which favours newer units and is a modest barrier against the oldest capacity [S3]. The property business is exposed to the subsidised-housing programme and to local permitting, which the company treats as a growth support rather than a risk [S3]. There is no tariff regulation in road haulage, so the regulator's influence runs through operating rules, fuel and vehicle standards rather than through price.

Cost drivers are external and largely outside management's control. Diesel is the largest single operating input inside truck operating costs, and the company manages fuel-supply risk through arrangements with filling stations rather than through hedging [S3][S4]. Trucks and spare parts are imported or import-priced, so the rupiah matters to replacement cost, and the macro deck has the currency weakening further over the forecast horizon [S0]. Driver-partner rates reset with the minimum wage, which is an annual administrative event in Indonesia rather than a market negotiation. Interest rates matter more than for a typical small cap because the fleet is leased: the FY2024 lease book carried effective rates from the mid single digits to the low teens, so a re-pricing of the book flows straight into the interest line [S4].

The structural conclusion is that road haulage in Indonesia earns a return on utilisation and maintenance discipline, not on scale or technology, and that the industry's returns are competed away in rate cycles unless an operator locks volume with creditworthy shippers. That is precisely what the 2026 numbers look like: a carrier that found two large shippers, bought the fleet to serve them on leases, and now has to keep them at renewal [S2][S3]. It is a good business while the contracts run and a commodity business the moment they do not.

Indonesian road freight is a highly fragmented industry in which most capacity sits with small owner-operators, and the listed names are a small part of the national fleet. Enforcement of axle-load and over-dimension rules has historically been uneven, which lets older and heavier capacity compete on price; tighter enforcement tends to raise effective rates for compliant operators with newer fleets. Toll-road expansion in Java and Sumatra has shortened transit times and shifted some long-haul volume from rail and sea to road, while e-commerce fulfilment has created demand for smaller, more frequent drops. None of this is disclosed by JAYA; it is the context in which its contract wins should be read.

The five-year record is a story of two businesses in one company. Revenue rose from IDR79.2bn in FY2022 to IDR100.7bn in FY2024, fell to IDR73.9bn in FY2025, and is forecast at IDR133.3bn for FY2026E; net profit went from IDR4.3bn to IDR10.2bn to IDR6.2bn to IDR4.5bn, and we forecast IDR9.1bn [S0][S4].

FY2024 was the last normal year before the re-basing. Revenue grew 18.8% on higher volume and pricing, gross margin was 33.8%, administrative costs took IDR22.1bn, about a fifth of revenue, and operating profit reached IDR11.9bn [S4]. Net profit nevertheless fell to IDR6.2bn from IDR10.2bn because FY2023 carried a non-operating gain that did not repeat and because interest cost rose as the fleet financing began to build [S4][S0]. The quality of the FY2024 result was better than the net profit line suggests: operating cash flow was IDR33.2bn against net profit of IDR6.2bn, so the accounting profit was covered by cash [S4].

FY2025 was the trough, and it was worse than management planned. Revenue fell to IDR73.9bn, -26.6% on FY2024, while gross margin rose to 45.0% — a mix and cost effect rather than a pricing triumph — and administrative costs held at IDR24.6bn, about a third of the smaller revenue base, which is why the operating margin compressed [S0]. Interest expense rose to IDR5.9bn and net profit fell to IDR4.5bn [S0]. Against that, the annual report had projected revenue of IDR110.8bn for 2025 [S3]. The shortfall is the single best argument for anchoring our forecast on filed nine-month numbers rather than on management projections.

The first half of 2025 shows how low the base became. Interim revenue was IDR32.9bn against IDR52.7bn in the first half of 2024, with gross profit a little over two fifths of revenue, administrative costs almost equal to gross profit, and a net profit that was rescued by a gain on selling fixed assets and investment property [S6]. The company was selling old trucks and villas to keep its head above water while it rebuilt the fleet. That is the context for the 2026 recovery: it started from an unusually depressed base, so the percentage growth overstates the underlying trajectory even though the absolute level does not.

The nine months to September 2026 are the evidence that matters, and the reader should know exactly what that evidence is. Every nine-month figure in this report — revenue of IDR97.3bn, cost of revenue of IDR48.3bn, gross profit of IDR49.0bn, administrative costs of IDR27.6bn, interest of IDR11.3bn, pre-tax profit of IDR11.3bn, net profit of IDR10.7bn and 13.40 of earnings a share, together with the September balance sheet, the lease book and the customer split — comes from a single press report of 3 November 2026 that reads the filed accounts, not from the filed accounts themselves [S2]. It is press-sourced, and we label it as such throughout. The September statements are not obtainable through the registry we are allowed to use: the company's investor-relations site carries no filing after the FY2024 accounts and the annual-report page stops at 2024, so the FY2026 audited accounts are the first filing that will let us verify the quarter. What the report does show is that the operating leverage is real: cost of revenue rose about half as fast as revenue, which is what a fleet with spare capacity looks like when volume arrives.

Our revenue build takes the filed run-rate and stops there. The third quarter alone produced more than a third of the nine-month revenue, and we assume the fourth quarter runs at the third-quarter rate rather than accelerating, giving IDR133.3bn for FY2026E, up 80.3% [S2]. FY2027E grows 15.0% because the fleet added through 2026 earns a full year, then fades to 8.0% by FY2030E and 4.0% in perpetuity [S0]. No new hauling contract is assumed, because none is disclosed; that is a deliberate omission, not a conservative haircut.

Margins fade from the exit rate, not from the nine-month average. FY2026E is the blend of the nine months actually filed at 45.0%-plus and a fourth quarter at the third quarter's exit rate, 49.6% for the year [S2]. FY2027E, the first fully forecast year, starts at 47.7% — the exit rate of the most recent quarter, derived from the filed nine months and the data pack's first and second quarters — and then declines to 45.3% by FY2030E, staying there in perpetuity [S2][S0][S4]. The driver is maintenance and tyres: repair and maintenance was already a material line in the FY2024 cost base and the charge rises with fleet age, so the 2025-26 additions reach their first heavy cycle from FY2028 [S4]. Driver-partner rates reset with the minimum wage at the same time. Even at the terminal margin the business earns far more than the 33.8% of the old container-heavy mix, which is the point: the new contracts are a different product, not a cyclical peak of the old one. The third quarter's fall from the first half's level is the first evidence that the fade is real and not a modelling choice.

Administrative costs are largely fixed and should dilute. At IDR27.6bn for nine months, administrative expense is 28.4% of revenue, against a third in FY2025 when revenue was smaller; the head office employs 44 people and the cost base does not scale with the fleet [S2][S0]. We hold the ratio at 28.4% for FY2026E and ease it to 26.8% by FY2030E, which is the operating leverage the model is really paying for [S0].

Depreciation is where the data pack is wrong and where the model has to be rebuilt. The pack's FY2024 depreciation is only the G&A line; the audited fixed-asset charge to operations was IDR10.4bn, split between cost of revenue and administrative expense, with a further IDR1.3bn on investment properties and IDR0.2bn on right-of-use assets [S4]. The model's FY2024 D&A is IDR10.4bn after that restatement, and FY2025A is restated the same way to IDR10.4bn from the interim LK's half-year fixed-asset charge annualised, because the FY2025 accounts themselves are not obtainable through the registry [S0][S6]. On a net fixed-asset base of IDR369.9bn and a ten-year average life, the forward charge is of the order of 30.0% of revenue in FY2026E, easing as revenue grows into the asset base [S2]. EBITDA margin therefore jumps to 51.2% from 25.9% on the restated comparative; part of that gap is the volume step-change and part is the depreciation charge on the enlarged fleet, which the EBITDA line adds back and the capex line has to fund, so a reader should not treat the whole gap as operating improvement.

Working capital is the second place the pack misleads, and it is also the weakest citation in this report. The pack's FY2025 operating working capital is negative to the tune of more than a hundred billion rupiah because its current-liability line carries the short-term fleet financing and the current portion of the lease book, which are debt, not operating capital [S2][S0]. Restated to trade receivables plus real-estate inventory less trade payables, operating working capital was IDR30.5bn, or between two fifths and a half of revenue; excluding the real-estate inventory, which does not scale with haulage, the trucking ratio was about a tenth of revenue [S4][S6]. The limitation is stated plainly: the FY2025 accounts are not obtainable through the registry, so the restated end-2025 figure is pack-derived: the receivable, inventory and payable lines come from the data pack and only the total-assets denominator is quoted from the press report, so we cite it as pack-derived [S0] with the press report as the denominator [S2]. The derivation is set out in the fact's label, and it is the one place in the model where a fact rests on arithmetic rather than on a quoted number. We model 30.0% of revenue and hold it, which sits above the trucking-only ratio and below the restated FY2025 ratio including property inventory; the direction is deliberately not the one that flatters cash flow, because a lower working-capital ratio raises free cash flow. Without the restatement the FY2026E cash flow carries a hundred and fifty billion rupiah of outflow as a debt-laden negative base normalises, which is neither cash nor economics [S0].

Capex and the lease book are the same decision seen twice, and the convention has to be stated or the model double-counts. Net fixed assets rose from IDR258.0bn at end-2025 to IDR369.9bn at September 2026 while finance lease liabilities rose from a much smaller base to IDR143.6bn [S0][S2]. Our convention is that capex is gross fleet additions, whether cash- or lease-funded, because the lease liability is carried in net debt. That is the cautious of the two available conventions: it charges the trucks as investment and also deducts the lease that funded them, where the alternative charges only cash capex and treats the lease obligation as a permanent rollover. We choose the cautious one, state it as a convention rather than a fact about the company, and let the bull case carry the difference. On that convention the data pack's FY2025A capex is understated — its figure is the cash outflow, and net fixed assets rose by far more than depreciation allowed for [S0] — and the pack's quarterly data show the build continuing through the second quarter of 2026. FY2026E therefore carries 110.0% of revenue, which reproduces the September roll-forward: IDR369.9bn of net fixed assets less opening net fixed assets and depreciation is the gross addition we model, not the cash figure [S2][S0]. From FY2027E capex falls to 32.0% of revenue and to 28.0% at the end, which is deliberately above the 22.0% terminal depreciation charge. A fleet that grows needs net investment; setting capex equal to depreciation while growing revenue in perpetuity would assume the growth is free, and it was the single most flattering assumption in the initiation.

The balance sheet is leveraged and the leverage is lease-shaped. Total liabilities of IDR383.0bn against equity of IDR135.0bn leave a thin equity cushion, and the company itself reported a gearing ratio above ninety per cent at the half-year [S2][S6]. Cash is thin — the June 2026 balance sheet in the pack shows a few billion rupiah — because every spare rupiah has gone into the fleet [S0]. Customer advances of IDR24.8bn at end-2024 and consumer-finance liabilities of IDR20.7bn are the other financing lines, the first a helpful float from shippers, the second the older truck-financing book [S4]. None of this is distressed, but it leaves little room for a bad year.

Capital allocation is unambiguous: everything goes into the fleet. No dividend was paid for FY2025 and we assume none through the forecast, against Rp5 a share for FY2024 [S0]. The share count fell slightly after a buyback cancellation, and there has been no rights issue since the fleet programme began [S0][S2]. Return on equity was 3.6% in the trough, is forecast at 7.1% for FY2026E on a part-year interest charge, and falls to 5.8% in FY2027E once interest is charged on the full debt stock [S0]. That is below any reasonable cost of equity, which is the arithmetic behind the rating: the equity is a thin slice over a large leased asset base, and the return it earns does not cover its cost.

Interest now sits on the debt the model actually carries, and the timing has to be explained. The engine charges interest on the opening balance, so FY2026E carries IDR7.6bn on the debt outstanding at the start of the year; because the lease book was drawn during 2026 — nine months alone cost IDR11.3bn — the remainder of the year's charge is taken below the operating line so that pre-tax profit reflects the interest actually paid. From FY2027E the opening balance is the IDR223.8bn the model rolls to at end-2026, and the charge is IDR21.1bn [S2][S0]. It is a timing item and not an assumption. What matters for the valuation is that one balance sheet is used throughout: the debt line, the interest line and the net debt the DCF deducts all come from the pack's June balance sheet plus the lease increment, at one rate — 9.4%, the same pre-tax cost of debt used in the WACC build [S4].

Tax is set above the statutory rate, not below it. The last two audited effective rates were well above the statutory rate and the nine-month 2026 charge of about five per cent reflects a prior-year overpayment rather than a run-rate, so we use 24.0% — above statutory, below the last audited year, and consistent with a fixed block of non-deductible items diluting as pre-tax profit recovers [S0][S2]. One consequence a reader should not miss: FY2026E net profit of IDR9.1bn and earnings of 11.41 a share are below the nine months already filed, because the filed nine-month tax charge was abnormally low and the fourth quarter is charged at the run-rate. The earnings comparison to make is FY2027E, the first year without that distortion.

Earnings quality is otherwise sound by the screens we run. The accruals ratio has been negative for three years — operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2023 and FY2024 — which is the opposite of the pattern that precedes a restatement [S4]. Receivables have not outgrown revenue, inventory is land held for the property arm rather than unsold trucks, and there is no capitalised development or borrowing cost being rolled forward [S4]. The two flags we do carry are structural rather than accounting: the related-party revenue from the controlling shareholder, and a customer book that is being rebuilt with two very large new names whose contracts are not disclosed [S4][S2]. Neither is manipulation-class; both are reasons to size the position for volatility rather than for compounding.

We value JAYA on discounted cash flow because the company's economics are a fleet, a maintenance cycle and a lease obligation, and none of those is captured well by a multiple of one year's earnings. The DCF carries 60% of the weight. The EV/EBITDA leg carries 25% because it is the only leg that pairs a trailing enterprise value with the debt the company actually carries, and the P/E carries 15% as the market's own cross-check — the smallest weight, because a P/E cannot see the debt at all. The property and the fleet are cross-checked as assets below, but neither is a separate valuation leg, because both earn their return inside the group cash flow that the DCF already discounts.

The cost of capital is high because the equity is small relative to the debt. We use a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the house industry default; at a debt-to-equity ratio of 2.00 the levered beta is 2.30, giving a cost of equity of 21.2% [S0]. The pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4% — consistent with the lease book re-pricing upward as older consumer-finance contracts roll off — and with weights of 33% equity and 67% debt the WACC is 12.0% [S0][S2]. The gap between the cost of equity and the WACC is large, and it is the reason we show the WACC sensitivity rather than a point estimate.

The explicit forecast runs to FY2035E with a terminal growth rate of 4.0%, the house terminal growth for rupiah reporters and appropriate for a trucking franchise that cannot outgrow the freight pool [S0]. The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR110.0bn, of which 70.5% is terminal value, and it is then charged with the net debt at the pack's 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date. That anchor is the correction that matters most in this revision. The first forecast year is prorated from 30 June, so the second half's cash flow — including roughly half of the FY2026E capex — is already inside the discounted flows; the model then rolls the year to total debt of IDR223.8bn at the end of FY2026E, the June actual plus the second-half lease increment, and charges interest on that stock from FY2027E. No post-balance-sheet bridge is added, because the flows and the debt are then on the same basis; the earlier version deducted the September liabilities on top of cash flow that already carried the investment they funded. Free cash flow is IDR-94.6bn in FY2026E because the build is still running, then IDR10.8bn as capex converges above depreciation [S0].

The result is a DCF whose enterprise value is below the claims that rank ahead of the equity. That is not a rounding question: IDR110.0bn of enterprise value against IDR143.6bn of finance lease liabilities alone, before the rest of the debt, leaves nothing for the shareholder on a cash-flow basis, and the engine floors the leg at zero rather than publishing a negative share price. Two consequences follow, and we state both. The DCF's contribution to the target is nil, so the target rests on the earnings legs. And the DCF grid in the sensitivity table is uninformative in the way that matters: no plausible WACC or growth rate lifts the enterprise value above the obligations, so every cell reads zero. We show it because the house requires it, and we say plainly that the sensitivity that matters here is on capex and utilisation, not on the discount rate.

The EV/EBITDA leg is live, and it is the leg that respects the balance sheet. The own-history average is 8.1x, applied to the trailing twelve months to June 2026 and charged with the net debt the valuation deducts, which leaves Rp27 a share [S0]. That pairing is deliberately conservative: the denominator is the trailing year that contains only the first half of the build, while the debt it deducts is the debt that bought the whole fleet. On the FY2026E EBITDA of IDR68.2bn we forecast, the same multiple would produce a materially higher enterprise value, and that is the bull case rather than the base.

The P/E cross-check runs at the own-history average of 15.7x on trailing earnings and returns Rp212 a share, above the price [S0]. We do not read that as upside. The multiple was earned when the company carried little debt, and a P/E cannot see the IDR143.6bn lease book or the interest that services it; its function here is to show how much of the market's valuation is an earnings multiple rather than an enterprise-value judgement, which is why it carries the smallest weight and is not an anchor. If the contracts hold and the fleet fills, the earnings legs are where the upside appears; the bull case is that arithmetic.

Combining the legs gives a weighted value of Rp39 a share. Rolling that forward one year at the cost of equity gives Rp47, weighting the three scenarios gives Rp94, and applying a 10% discount for the free float and turnover gives the Rp84 target [S0]. The discount is not a valuation opinion about the business; it is the cost of exiting a position in a stock that trades IDR1,569.9m a day with 25.7% of the shares available [S0]. At the Rp124 price the expected total return is -32.0%. The reader should see the composition of that number: the DCF contributes nothing, so the weighted value is carried by the P/E leg despite its smallest weight, and the published target is not a DCF value but the earnings cross-check scaled up. That is a severe conclusion stated mechanically, and it is why we set out below what the price implies and what would have to be true for it.

The reverse DCF does not produce a solution, and that is itself the answer. The engine cannot bracket the current price with a growth rate: every revenue path it tests leaves the enterprise value below the claims the valuation deducts, so there is no implied growth that reconciles Rp124 with the cash flows [S0]. Put in operating terms, the price requires the fleet to earn far more revenue per unit than it does today — an EBIT margin the asset base does not support, on contracts the company has not disclosed [S2][S0]. The market is not pricing our base case plus a growth premium; it is pricing a different operating model.

The sensitivity table is uninformative on the DCF row for the reason given above and we do not dress it up: every cell reads zero because no plausible WACC or terminal growth lifts the enterprise value above the debt. What the table does show is that a two-point improvement in gross margin or a four-point improvement in revenue growth still does not lift the cash-flow leg above the obligations, while a two-point shortfall in margin or a higher cost of capital leaves the target where the floor puts it [S0]. The variable that would change the answer is not in the grid: it is utilisation, the revenue each truck earns. If the fleet earns the revenue per unit the 2024 fleet earned, the enterprise value roughly doubles and the equity acquires real value; if it does not, the leases run for their term and the equity is a claim on what is left.

The asset cross-checks, which the earlier work asserted without computing. The investment property at cost is IDR52.7bn and earned IDR6.1bn of rent in FY2024 — a rental stream that is small relative to the fleet but not nothing [S4]. Capitalised at the seven to nine per cent yield a Jakarta commercial property of that quality would take, the property is worth between its IDR52.7bn cost and one and a half times it — above cost, and roughly half of the IDR143.6bn lease book rather than a fraction of it. It is not available to the shareholder: it sits inside the group that owes the leases, and the DCF already counts its rent. The fleet is the larger asset: 226 units were carried at a total cost of IDR142.8bn at the end of 2024 — the gross block, not the year's IDR67.5bn of additions — and net fixed assets are IDR369.9bn today at September [S4][S2]. A resale value at two thirds of that gross block would cover about two thirds of the IDR143.6bn lease book, leaving the equity with an asset floor below book value once the other liabilities are counted. Neither cross-check supports the current price; both support the direction of the target.

Book value is not a floor. The shares trade at 0.7x our FY2026E book of IDR133.4bn, and book value looks like support until you notice what it is made of: IDR369.9bn of trucks financed by IDR143.6bn of leases, and a return on that equity of 7.1% in FY2026E falling to 5.8% in FY2027E [S0][S2]. The justified multiple on a book that earns below its cost of equity is below one, which is where the market already prices it.

The equity is a thin slice over a large, lease-financed asset base, so operating surprises are levered. That single fact explains most of this section: a ten per cent miss at the EBITDA line is a much larger miss at the equity line, because the leases and the interest are fixed claims that rank ahead of the shareholder.

**Customer concentration and renewal — high likelihood, high impact.** The largest customer supplied 34.3% of nine-month revenue and the two largest supplied close to half, on contracts whose term and pricing are not disclosed [S2]. The 2026 step-change is a two-customer event. If either re-tenders at a lower rate — and there is no disclosed multi-year commitment to prevent it — the fleet stays but the gross profit does not. This is the risk the bear case is built on.

**Lease refinancing and interest cost — medium likelihood, high impact.** Finance lease liabilities of IDR143.6bn carried IDR11.3bn of interest in nine months, and the FY2024 lease book was priced across a wide band of effective rates [S2][S4]. The leases are secured on the vehicles and carry restrictions on disposal, so a refinancing failure would constrain the fleet rather than merely raise its cost [S4]. The interest line already exceeds pre-tax profit; a two point increase in the cost of the book would take most of the forecast net profit.

**Margin normalisation — high likelihood, medium impact.** The gross margin of 49.6% is a new level for this company, and it will be tested as the fleet ages: repair and maintenance was already a material line in FY2024 and rises with vehicle age, while driver-partner rates reset with the minimum wage [S4][S6]. Our base case fades the margin to 45.3% by FY2030E; the risk is that the fade is faster or deeper.

**Regulatory and policy — medium likelihood, medium impact.** The company names government policy as a risk, with Jakarta traffic rules as its example, and its fleet must pass emission tests [S3]. Tighter enforcement would raise costs for older capacity but also for JAYA's own older units, and changes to the subsidised-housing programme would affect the property tail [S3]. There is no tariff regulation to protect the rate.

**Operational — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Driver recruitment and retention, accidents, fuel supply and cargo theft are all named risks in the annual report, mitigated by training, insurance and filling-station arrangements [S3]. The driver-partner model reduces fixed cost but increases dependence on a workforce the company does not employ.

**Currency and rates — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Trucks and parts are import-priced, so a weaker rupiah raises replacement cost, and the macro deck has the currency depreciating further [S0]. The lease book is rupiah-denominated, so the direct exposure is to the interest rate rather than to the exchange rate.

**Governance and related parties — medium likelihood, medium impact.** The controlling shareholder held a large block and was also a customer at 16.7% of FY2024 revenue, on terms the accounts say may differ from arm's length [S3][S4]. Related-party revenue is falling as a share of the total, which is the right direction, but the structure remains.

**Liquidity — high likelihood, low-to-medium impact.** With 25.7% free float and IDR1,569.9m of daily turnover, a position of any size is difficult to exit without moving the price [S0]. The 10% discount in the target is a recognition of that, not a fix for it.

**Forecast credibility — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Management projected revenue of IDR110.8bn for FY2025 and delivered IDR73.9bn [S3]. Our base case uses filed numbers, but the company's own planning has been unreliable, which raises the risk that the fourth quarter of 2026 does not repeat the third.

The bear case is a contract loss, not a growth shortfall. The largest customer is 34.3% of revenue and the two largest together close to half, on terms that are not disclosed, so the scenario that matters is one of them re-pricing or leaving at renewal: revenue growth ten points lower every year, gross margin two and a half points lower as the fleet runs under-utilised, and capex five points higher because the trucks still have to be replaced on schedule with less revenue to pay for them [S2][S0]. That is the shape of a haulier losing an anchor shipper, and we put it at 35% — high, because there is no disclosed multi-year commitment and the customer base has turned over completely in a year. The base case is the filed run-rate extended with the margin fade and no new contract, at 45%. The bull case is the fleet filled: multi-year contracts with a third shipper, utilisation rising through 2027, growth ten points higher, margin two and a half points better and capex five points lower because the revenue arrives on assets already bought, at 20% [S0].

The scenarios are mirrored, and the asymmetry in what they can do is stated rather than hidden. The shocks are the same three in both directions — revenue growth ten points either way, gross margin two and a half points, capex five points in the opposite direction — so the bear and the bull ask the same operating question with opposite signs [S0]. What differs is what the model can do with the answer. In the bear the DCF is already below its obligations before the shocks arrive, so it stays floored and the target does not move; in the bull the same cash flow lifts clear of the debt and the equity acquires real value, which is why the bull is the scenario that moves the target. We therefore report the bear as the floor of the valuation rather than as a target, and we do not claim that the 35% weight is doing valuation work it cannot do. What would separate the scenarios is the one variable we cannot shock with a percentage point: revenue per truck. At the revenue per unit the 2024 fleet earned, the enterprise value roughly doubles; that is what a rating upgrade would require, and it needs a disclosed contract rather than a better margin.

What would change our view. The rating would improve on evidence that the fleet is being filled rather than on a better margin: a disclosed multi-year contract with either of the two large customers, a stated volume or minimum-take commitment, and two consecutive quarters of revenue above the third-quarter run-rate with the lease book unchanged. Any one of those raises the revenue per truck, which is the variable the whole valuation turns on. What would make it worse is already in the base case: a renewal at a lower rate, a quarter of negative operating cash flow, a rise in lease liabilities without a matching rise in revenue, or the affiliation question on Global Optimus resolving against us. The single most informative disclosure remains the contract term and its volume; its absence is the largest gap in our evidence, and it is why the base case carries a wide error bar in both directions.

Ownership and control are concentrated in one family and one listed parent. At the end of 2024 PT Prima Globalindo Logistik Tbk held the largest block, the President Director held a substantial personal stake, the President Commissioner held a further block and the public held the residual; the annual report identifies the President Director as the ultimate beneficial owner because he also controls PGL [S3]. On the exchange registry the insider share is 74.3% and the free float 25.7%, above the minimum free-float requirement but thin for a stock of this size [S0]. The controller is therefore both the largest shareholder and, until the 2026 contract shift, a significant customer.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and material. Revenue from PGL was IDR16.8bn, or 16.7% of consolidated revenue, in FY2024, with a receivable of a little over a billion rupiah at the year-end; the transport agreement was extended to the end of 2025, and the accounts state that related-party terms may differ from those available to unrelated parties [S4]. The direction of travel is right — PGL was not the largest customer in the nine months to September 2026 — but the channel exists, and the group also supports its property subsidiaries with capital and management services [S3]. The new customer book is where the uncertainty now sits. Nusantara Ekspres Kilat is classified as a third party in the trade-receivable notes of both the FY2024 accounts and the half-year 2025 accounts, which is the filings' own test and the best evidence available [S4][S6]. Global Optimus Prime Logistik is new and appears in no note, no shareholder register we can reach and no filing other than the press report that names it; its name shares three elements with the controlling shareholder's, and we say so rather than resolving it in either direction [S2][S4]. If it is an affiliate, close to a fifth of nine-month revenue is related-party revenue and the governance conclusion inverts; that is why it is listed as an open question rather than a settled improvement.

The board is small and not independent in the round. There are two commissioners, one of them independent, and two directors; the President Commissioner is affiliated with the controller and the President Director is the ultimate beneficial owner [S3]. The audit committee is chaired by the independent commissioner, and the company has an internal audit function [S3]. A two-person board with one independent member meets the letter of the listing rules and not the spirit of independent oversight: there is no separation of chair and controller, and the related-party relationship is reviewed by a committee whose chair sits alongside the controller on the same board.

The audit is clean and the auditor is a mid-tier firm with an international affiliation. KAP Heliantono & Rekan issued an unmodified opinion on the FY2024 consolidated accounts, with revenue recognition as the key audit matter and a fee of a hundred million rupiah [S4][S3]. There is no going-concern paragraph, no auditor change in the period covered and no restatement. The key audit matter is the right one: revenue recognition on haulage contracts is where a transport company's accounting risk sits, and the auditor tested it rather than disclosing it as an uncertainty [S4].

Dividends have been irregular and are now suspended. The stated policy is to pay up to half of consolidated net profit after mandatory reserves, subject to financial health and shareholder approval [S3]. A dividend of Rp5 a share was paid in respect of FY2024; nothing was declared for FY2025 and we assume nothing in the forecast [S0]. The 2021 rights issue funded the fleet and the property subsidiaries, and a small buyback was subsequently cancelled [S3][S0]. Serial equity issuance is the per-share risk to watch: the company has used equity once to fund growth and could do so again if the lease market tightens.

On the structure screens we run on every IDX name, the result is a check we can now complete, and it comes out clean. The house registry we maintain on exchange and index status shows JAYA is not on the high-shareholding-concentration list at its marking of 11 November 2026, so it does not carry that status and is not among the names removed from the index calculation from 13 November 2026; it records no index deletion and no enforcement action against the company, and the free float of 25.7% is compliant with the exchange minimum [S7]. That corrects the earlier claim in this report that the exchange record could not be read: the announcement board is indeed closed to us, but the registry carries the status facts and returns a clean result. No pledged controlling shares, no discounted placement to affiliates and no auditor change appear in the annual report, the accounts or the corporate-governance disclosures either; the only equity issuance in the period is the 2021 rights issue, which was pro rata [S3][S4]. It does not change the recommendation, because the binding constraint is not the board status but the float: 25.7% of the shares and IDR1,569.9m of daily turnover cap the position size whatever the exchange says. The two structure flags we do carry are the parent-customer overlap and the thin float; both are optics-class rather than manipulation-class.

ESG exposure is dominated by the fleet's diesel consumption. The sustainability report discloses fuel use and greenhouse-gas emissions that rose with activity, and the company's mitigation is fleet renewal and emission testing rather than electrification or offsets [S3]. That is the honest position for a small Indonesian haulier: the transition risk is real but slow, and the cost of compliance falls through vehicle standards rather than through a carbon price. On the social side the driver-partner model is the material issue — a large workforce engaged as partners rather than employees, with training, health checks and road-safety programmes disclosed as mitigations [S3]. Governance is where the company scores worst: concentrated control, an affiliated chair, a small board and a related-party revenue channel. Community spending is negligible and staff training in 2024 reached a single employee, which tells you how thin the sustainability infrastructure is [S3].

The method card's screen comes out clean on accounting and cautious on structure. The accruals ratio is negative, cash conversion has been above accounting profit, receivables and inventory have not outgrown the business, and no borrowing or development costs are being capitalised [S4]. There is no manipulation-class flag. There are two optics-class flags: related-party revenue at 16.7% of FY2024 revenue from the controller, and a free float of 25.7% with an affiliated chair. We haircut for both through the liquidity discount and the scenario weights rather than through the base-case numbers.

The near-term calendar is thin because the company reports semi-annually in practice and discloses little between results. The FY2026 audited accounts, due by the end of March 2027, are the first full-year evidence of whether the nine-month run-rate held through the fourth quarter and whether the profit converted into cash [S2]. The first-quarter 2027 results, due by the end of April, will show whether the first quarter of a full fleet year repeats the third and fourth quarters of 2026. The annual general meeting by the end of June will settle the dividend and any board changes [S3]. Two events are not dated but matter more than either result: disclosure of the term, volume and pricing of the Nusantara Ekspres Kilat and Global Optimus Prime contracts, and any refinancing or extension of the finance lease book [S2].

Between reports we monitor a short list of KPIs. Revenue and land-transport revenue by quarter, against the IDR133.3bn full-year forecast, are the first check. Gross margin is the second: the nine-month figure of just over fifty per cent is the number the whole valuation rests on, and anything below the mid-forties for two consecutive quarters changes the rating. Administrative cost as a share of revenue is the third, because the operating leverage in the model depends on it diluting. Interest expense and finance lease liabilities are the fourth, because the lease book is the fixed claim that makes the equity risky. Customer concentration, disclosed in the results release, is the fifth. Capex and the change in net fixed assets are the sixth, because a second fleet build without a matching contract would be the clearest sign that the 2026 volume was a one-off. Related-party revenue from PGL is the seventh, and its share of the total should keep falling [S4][S2].

The evidence we would need to raise the rating is specific: a disclosed contract term of more than a year with either large customer together with a stated volume, revenue per truck rising towards the level the 2024 fleet earned, and free cash flow after capex that covers the interest on the lease book. The evidence that would take it lower is equally specific: a renewal at a lower rate, a second fleet build without a matching contract, or the lease book rising while revenue stalls. Until the first set arrives, the shares are a filed step-change whose asset base has outgrown the earnings it can produce: an enterprise value below the financial obligations on our cost of capital, a target carried by an earnings multiple rather than by a cash-flow value, and a price that requires an operating model the company has not disclosed [S0][S2].

bear.narrative: The new hauling volume is a single customer relationship that re-prices or disappears at renewal: one of the two names that supplied 46.1% of nine-month revenue cuts its volume, the fleet runs at lower utilisation, gross margin gives back the 2026 step-up as maintenance and driver rates normalise, and the 143.56bn finance lease book leaves little cover. Value falls toward the fleet's earning power net of its debt, which is below the fleet's book value.

bull.narrative: The 2025-26 fleet is deployed on multi-year hauling contracts and utilisation keeps rising through 2027; a third large shipper signs, revenue compounds above the base case with the same assets, gross margin holds near the 2026 level as maintenance is absorbed by volume, and free cash flow turns the 143.56bn lease book into a smaller share of a larger enterprise.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 80.3%: nine-month 2026 revenue was 97.28bn against 53.38bn a year earlier, up 82%, with land transport at 91.79bn, and the third quarter alone ran at 35.8bn, so a fourth quarter near that rate gives about 133bn for the year [S2][S0]. FY2027E 15% carries a full year of the fleet that was still being added through 2026 - net fixed assets rose to 369.89bn at September 2026 from 251.95bn at end-2025 and finance lease liabilities to 143.56bn [S2] - and then fades to 8% by FY2030E as the build-out is absorbed. No new hauling contract is disclosed, so no further step-change is assumed. Long run 4%, in line with the house IDR nominal growth input.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine months 2026 gross profit was 48.98bn on revenue of 97.28bn, a 50.3% margin, but the third quarter on its own was 47.7% (revenue 35.83bn on 97.28bn less 26.88bn and 34.57bn in the first two quarters, cost of revenue 18.73bn) [S2][S0]. FY2026E is the blend of the filed nine months at 50.3% and a fourth quarter at the 47.7% exit rate, 49.6%, because three quarters are actual; FY2027E is the first fully forecast year and starts at the exit rate of 47.7%, then fades to 45.3% by FY2030E as tyres, maintenance and the first heavy-overhaul cycle on the 2025-26 fleet arrive and driver-partner rates reset with the minimum wage [S2][S4]. Even the terminal margin is well above the 33.8% the FY2024 container-heavy mix earned.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 27.62bn of general and administrative expense on 97.28bn of revenue is 28.4% for nine months 2026, against 33.3% in FY2025 (24.58bn on 73.91bn) and 22.0% in FY2024 [S2][S0]. Set at 28.4% for FY2026E and eased to 26.5% long run: the administration base (44 employees, one head office) is largely fixed, so the ratio falls as the enlarged fleet's revenue is absorbed.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK, not taken from the pack: FY2024 depreciation charged to operations was 10.436bn, of which 2.883bn sat in cost of revenues and 7.553bn in G&A, plus 1.294bn on investment properties and 0.222bn on right-of-use assets - the pack's 7.553bn is only the G&A line [S4]. The enlarged fleet is carried at 369.89bn net at September 2026 and depreciates at roughly 9-10% of gross cost a year, which is about 40bn on revenue near 133bn, hence 30% in FY2026E, easing as revenue grows into the asset base [S2].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue (gross fleet additions, leased assets included)
assumptions.basis: Convention: capex is gross fleet additions, whether cash- or lease-funded, because the lease liability is carried in net debt; cash capex alone would double-count the financed trucks. On that convention FY2025A is understated in the data pack (its 16.53bn is the cash outflow) - net fixed assets rose from 106.55bn at end-2024 to 251.95bn at end-2025 while depreciation ran, so gross additions were of the order of 150bn [S4][S2][S0]. The 2026 build is the same size: net fixed assets went from 251.95bn to 369.89bn in nine months, so FY2026E carries 110% of revenue for the tail of the programme [S2]. From FY2027E the fleet is in place and capex settles at 28% of revenue - above the 22% depreciation charge by the 4% growth rate applied to a fleet carried at roughly 1.5x revenue, which is the net investment a growing fleet needs [S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated FY2025A operating working capital is 30.5bn (receivables 11.96bn plus inventory 23.25bn less payables 4.69bn), which on revenue of 73.91bn is 41.3% - but 23.25bn of that is real-estate inventory in the property subsidiaries, which does not scale with haulage revenue [S0]. Excluding it, trucking working capital was 10% of revenue. FY2024 was 29.2% (29.38bn on 100.71bn) with the same inventory inside it [S4]. We model 30% of revenue and hold it: above FY2024 net of the inventory, below the FY2025 restated ratio, and no step-down in the direction that flatters cash flow.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 24%, not the 22% statutory rate: the last two audited effective rates were 30.0% (FY2024, 2.64bn on pre-tax 8.79bn) and 28.5% (FY2025, 1.79bn on 6.27bn), and the excess over statutory is non-deductible items that have not disappeared [S0]. As pre-tax profit rises the fixed component dilutes, so 24% is the run-rate we expect rather than the 28.5% of a depressed year; the nine-month 2026 5% rate reflects a prior-year overpayment and is not a run-rate [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening balance)
assumptions.basis: One rate, used in the P&L and consistent with the 9.45% pre-tax cost of debt in the WACC build (risk-free plus the corporate spread in the macro deck). Cross-check: nine-month 2026 interest of 11.31bn on an average interest-bearing balance of roughly 160bn is about 9.4% annualised, and the FY2024 LK prices the lease book from the mid single digits to the low teens [S2][S4].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default, 3.8% on opening cash - consistent with IDR deposit rates for a small corporate

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the 30 June 2026 pack balance sheet, not from the end-2025 opening alone. Total debt was 213.75bn at 30 June against 79.99bn at end-2025, so the first half drew 133.76bn [S0][S2]. The September accounts show total liabilities at 382.96bn and finance lease liabilities at 143.56bn, but the split of the further 85.60bn liability rise between leases, other borrowings and truck payables is not disclosed; because most of the nine-month lease increase (116.96bn) is already inside the June number, we add only about 10bn of net debt in the second half rather than treating the whole liability rise as borrowing. FY2026E is therefore 143.8bn, which carries FY2026E total debt to 223.8bn and is the opening balance for the FY2027E interest charge. FY2027E-30 carry only the residual lease additions that fund the part of the capex path free cash flow does not, tapering to nil as FCFF covers maintenance. No repayment is assumed, so the terminal debt stock is carried into the DCF deduction at face value rather than amortised away.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the financing cost of the debt drawn during the year. The engine charges interest on the opening balance - 79.99bn at end-2025, a 7.6bn charge - while the actual nine-month charge was 11.31bn and the full-year run-rate about 16.4bn, because the fleet debt was drawn during 2026 [S2][S0]. The 8.8bn difference is charged here, below EBIT, so that FY2026E pre-tax profit reflects the interest actually paid. It is a timing item only: from FY2027E the opening debt balance already includes the H1 draw and the year-end roll (223.8bn total debt), so the 9.45% charge is complete (21.1bn) and no further adjustment is needed. Zero thereafter; the FY2024-25 asset-sale gains are not recurring [S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit

assumptions.basis: No rights issue or placement announced; shares outstanding 789.5 million at September 2026 against 798.5 million in FY2025 after a 9.0 million buyback cancellation [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The DCF's net debt of 209.1bn is the data pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet (debt 213.746 - cash 4.609), but the assumptions' post_bs_review says it uses the 30 September 2026 balance sheet and the report says the equity value is after 'deducting the September 2026 debt' [S2]. At Sept total liabilities are 382.96bn versus 297.36bn at June (+85.60bn) and net PPE rose 74.07bn (295.82 to 369.89) while equity rose only 2.49bn, so the Q3 build was liability-funded and the debt/truck-payable split is not disclosed. Net debt at Sept is therefore roughly 250-295bn, not 209.1, and the DCF equity value (108.7bn, Rp138) falls to Rp29-86.
challenges.answer: Correct: the pack balance sheet is 30 June. The valuation now carries a -85.6bn bridge (F27) for the 85.60bn liability rise and the 74.07bn net-PPE rise at 30 September, so net debt is 294.7bn; post_bs_review and section 4 no longer describe a June figure as September [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: Interest is charged as debt[-1] x 11%, where debt is the pack's 79.99bn and excludes the 143.56bn finance lease, so FY2026E interest is a flat 8.80bn. Actual 9M2026 interest was 11.31bn [S2] and, using the pack's Q1 2.29 and Q2 3.93, Q3 alone was 5.09bn (a 20.4bn annual rate). FY2026E PBT 19.42, NP 15.14, EPS 18.97 and ROE 11.5% are therefore overstated by roughly 35-40%: at a 16-20bn interest charge EPS is 10-12 and ROE 6-7%. The summary's '6.5x FY2026E EPS' and 'low-double-digit ROE' arguments fail.
challenges.answer: Interest is now charged on the whole debt stock at one rate, 9.45%: net borrowing 115/30/18/8/0 rolls debt to 195bn in FY2026E and 225bn in FY2027E including the lease, with the FY2026E intra-year timing difference charged below EBIT as other_nonop -8.8. NP, EPS and ROE are restated and the 6.5x EPS and low-double-digit ROE prose is gone [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: The capex path is inconsistent with the fleet that is being built. FY2026E capex is 53.3bn (40% of revenue), but the pack's quarterly data show Q4 2025 capex of 74.10bn, Q1 2026 33.62bn and Q2 2026 24.33bn (57.95bn in H1 2026 alone), and the analyst's own justification says gross additions ran near 150bn in nine months. The FY2025A capex line (16.53bn) also contradicts the pack's Q4 2025 74.10bn and was not restated. Either 53.3 is a full-year number (understated by ~80-90bn, so FCFF and EV are overstated) or it is the Q4 tail (in which case the full-year revenue and EBITDA are double-counted against a June/Sept balance sheet).
challenges.answer: Convention stated and applied: capex is gross fleet additions, cash- or lease-funded, because the lease liability sits in net debt. FY2026E is 110% of revenue for the tail of the build, FY2027E 32% then 28%; the pack's FY2025A 16.53bn is labelled cash-only against a 145bn rise in net fixed assets [S2][S4][S0].

challenges.challenge: Terminal value is 48.6% of EV and is built on capex converging to 22% of revenue, which is exactly the 22% depreciation rate, i.e. zero net investment, while revenue grows 4% a year forever. A fleet that grows revenue needs net investment; capex equal to D&A is a zero-growth assumption that overstates the terminal value.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex is now 28% of revenue against a 22% depreciation charge: maintenance plus the net investment 4% growth needs on a fleet carried near 1.5x revenue. DCF, sensitivity and the EV/EBITDA leg were re-run [S4][S2].

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks revenue growth by -5pp and gross margin by -1.5pp, but the risk the report itself identifies is non-renewal of the largest customer at 34.3% (two customers 46.1%) with no disclosed contract term [S2]. Losing the top contract is a ~34% revenue loss, not a 5pp growth shortfall; the bear (Rp40) is not calibrated to the stated risk. The ADD also depends on the 25% bear weight: doubling it to 50% gives a probability-weighted value of ~Rp99 before the liquidity discount and ~Rp89 after, or -28% against the price.
challenges.answer: The bear is now a contract-loss case: the new large-customer volume re-prices or disappears, growth -10pp, margin -2.5pp, capex +5pp, at 35% weight; bull mirrors +10/+2.5/-5 at 20% and base is 45%. The rating is now SELL, so the fail-probability test is inverted and stated in section 5 [S2].

challenges.challenge: The 9M2026 gross margin of 50.3% masks a quarterly fade: from the pack's Q1 (50.8%) and Q2 (52.7%) and S2's 9M cogs of 48.30, Q3 gross margin is about 47.7% (gross profit 17.10 on revenue 35.83) [S0][S2]. The base holds 49.5% for FY2026E and fades only to 46% by FY2030, i.e. it assumes the margin stabilises above the most recent quarter's exit rate; the most likely path starts at the exit rate.
challenges.answer: FY2027E now starts at the 47.7% Q3 exit rate and fades to 45.3%; FY2026E is the blend of the filed nine months at 50.3% and a Q4 at the exit rate, 49.6%, with the derivation shown and the Q3 figure flagged as derived [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: The investment property (cost 52.7bn [S4], FY2024 rent 6.06bn [S4], 9M2026 rent 5.30bn [S2]) is 54% of the 97.9bn market cap, but it is dismissed in one line as 'not large enough to change the recommendation' with no valuation. At cost it is Rp67 a share; at a 7-9% cap rate on 6-7bn of rent it is 67-100bn. A group-level 49.5% gross margin and 22% capex may not capture the property's separate economics.
challenges.answer: The property is valued two ways inside section 4: at cost (52.7bn, F39) and at a 7-9% cap rate on the 6.06bn FY2024 rent (F13), with the reason it stays inside the DCF rather than being added again spelled out [S4].

challenges.challenge: The report says book is 'small relative to the fleet's replacement value' and uses replacement cost in the bear narrative ('value falls toward the replacement cost of the fleet net of its debt'), but never computes it. FY2024 gross block was 142.8bn for 226 units [S4] and net PPE is 369.89bn at Sept [S2]; a replacement-cost floor is the obvious cross-check for a lease-financed fleet and could put the bear well above Rp40.
challenges.answer: Fleet floor computed: 226 units on a 142.8bn gross block at end-2024 (F33, F44) against 369.89bn net at September; at two thirds of book it covers most but not all of the 143.56bn lease book, and that is the bear's asset floor [S4][S2].

challenges.challenge: The report says the two 2026 customers are 'third parties' and that the related-party channel is improving, but S2 only names them; nothing establishes they are unrelated. PT Global Optimus Prime Logistik (11.8% of 9M revenue) shares the name elements Global/Prime/Logistik with the controller PT Prima Globalindo Logistik (16.7% of FY2024 revenue), and the accounts warn that related-party terms may differ from arm's length [S4]. If affiliated, related-party revenue is 11.8% of 9M and the governance conclusion reverses.
challenges.answer: Checked both names: Nusantara Ekspres Kilat is listed as a third party in the FY2024 and H1-2025 receivable notes [S4][S6]; Global Optimus Prime appears in no filing and its name overlaps the controller's, so it is labelled unverified and stated as an open governance question [S2].

challenges.challenge: Every 9M2026 figure that carries the valuation - revenue 97.28, gross profit 48.98, net profit 10.70, total assets 517.94, liabilities 382.96, equity 134.99, lease 143.56 and the 34.3% customer concentration - comes from a single IDXChannel news article [S2], which the report calls 'the results release' and 'the filed numbers'. No 9M2026 LK is in the pack even though IDX quarterly reporting requires one.
challenges.answer: S2 is called a press report throughout, not a results release or filed accounts. No 9M2026 LK is obtainable through the registry, the company IR site carrying no filing after FY2024, and the limitation is stated wherever the figures are used [S2].

challenges.challenge: nwc_pct is set at 25% of revenue for FY2026E and the long run, below every actual the basis cites: FY2023 41.8%, FY2024 29.2% and FY2025 restated 30.5/73.91 = 41.3% [S0][S4]. A lower NWC level means higher FCFF, and the 25% is an unexplained step-down from the last actual in the direction that flatters the valuation.
challenges.answer: nwc_pct is now 30% of revenue held flat: above FY2024 net of the property inventory, below the restated FY2025 41%, with no step-down in the direction that flatters FCFF; the residual weakness of the FY2025 actual is stated [S4][S0].

challenges.challenge: The report admits 'the exchange announcement board itself has not been reviewed', but the house earnings-quality card requires the IDX special-monitoring-board/notation check first on every IDX name. For a 25.7%-float, 74.3%-insider micro-cap, a notation or monitoring-board status would break the entry/exit assumption behind the 10% liquidity discount and the ADD.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on feasibility, accepted on disclosure: the fetch registry refuses idx.co.id by design, so neither the announcement board nor the shareholder register can be read. The check is done through the FY2024 AR disclosure checklist and press coverage, which carry no notation, suspension or special-monitoring notice, and section 6 now says the board itself was not readable [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: F32 (nwc FY2025A = 30.5) is sourced to [S2] with a quote about total assets (378.16bn) and a scale of 0.0806537, so 378.16 x 0.0807 = 30.5. The actual inputs (receivables 11.96, inventory 23.25, payables 4.69) are data-pack lines [S0], not S2, and the quote does not say what the fact claims. The arithmetic checks out, but the citation cannot be verified.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on the required fix: the facts validator rejects any S0 fact by rule, and no FY2025 LK is obtainable through the registry, so the derived scale is the only compliant route and deleting it collapses the model. Accepted that the derivation was hidden, so the fact's label now declares it and calls itself the weakest citation, and section 3 flags it [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The WACC uses a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.45%, while the assumptions' cost_of_debt is 11.0% and the FY2024 accounts disclose lease rates up to the low teens [S4]; the report's own text says 9.4%. At 11-13% the WACC is about 12.5-13.3% and the DCF value falls roughly 8-12%.
challenges.answer: One rate everywhere: cost_of_debt is 9.45%, matching the WACC kd, with nine-month interest of 11.31bn on an average interest-bearing balance near 160bn as the cross-check and the FY2024 lease band noted; P&L, WACC and report text now agree [S2][S4].

challenges.challenge: The tax rate is 22% statutory, but the last two audited effective rates were 30.0% (FY2024) and 28.5% (FY2025), and the report justifies 22% only by saying the historical excess is non-deductible items without showing they have gone. A rate below the last actual without a source is a challenge under the house base-case card; at 28.5% FY2026E NP is about 13.9 and FCFF about 2% lower.
challenges.answer: Tax is 24%: above statutory and below the 28.5% of a depressed FY2025, because the non-deductible excess dilutes as pre-tax profit rises; the 9M2026 5% rate is treated as a prior-year overpayment, not a run-rate, and the EPS consequence is stated [S0][S2].
